title: Handbook close
hook: fifty-three chapters in fifty-six days; the handbook is now yours to carry

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cleanthes, and the four old sayings that close the handbook. Your line was willingly. Which line steadied you? Day three hundred eighty-seven.

Fifty-three short sections in fifty-six days. That's the handbook, read in order, start to finish. Eight weeks ago we opened it with Arrian, the student who boiled his teacher's lessons down into a little book meant to be kept in the hand. The Greek name, enchiridion, means just that: the thing in the hand, a word also used for a small knife. Today we close it. Not to put it on a shelf. A handbook on a shelf has missed its whole point. Today: handbook close.
screen: `FIFTY-THREE SECTIONS, FIFTY-SIX DAYS.` → `THE THING IN THE HAND.` → `HANDBOOK CLOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the opening sorting. Section one split the world into two piles: what is up to us, our judgments, desires and choices, and what isn't, our body, property, reputation and office. Our line was start here. Almost everything after flowed from that one sort. Section five gave its sharpest form: people are disturbed not by things, but by their judgments about things. Second, the everyday tools. The jug you love is a jug. The baths will have splashing and shoving, so keep your purpose. When the dish comes around, take a modest share. You're an actor in a play; play your part well. The insult only harms through your judgment. Count the cost first. Third, living with other people. What the role asks. Mostly quiet. Yes means yes. Ask, don't tell. He missed the rest. The table matters. It seemed right to him. The other handle. Quickly, not badly. These can be the hardest to keep, because they happen in conversation, fast, with no time to look anything up. Fourth, the road. Signs of progress, starting with blame no one. Live the book, not just explain it. How long will you wait? And at the very end, Cleanthes: lead me on, and I'll follow willingly. Arrian made this book to be carried, and no one carries fifty-three things. So the last practice is a choice. Three sections. Three lines to keep in the hand. Tomorrow a new part of the path begins: the Discourses, the longer record of Epictetus actually teaching, joking and scolding in his classroom.
screen: `FIRST: WHAT IS UP TO US.` · `TOOLS: THE JUG, THE BATHS, THE BANQUET.` · `WITH OTHERS: THE OTHER HANDLE.` · `THE ROAD: BLAME NO ONE. WILLINGLY.` · then, large: `CARRY THREE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the eight weeks drift by: the two piles, the jug, the actor, the raven, the cup, the role, the quiet, the handles, the wool, the contest, the hymn. Don't chase any of them. Just notice which three keep coming back on their own. Those are yours. Say each one quietly, once. If you can, write them on something small enough to carry. The bell holds the time.
Enchiridion. The Greek name for the handbook, meaning the thing in the hand; fifty-three sections in fifty-six days, made to be carried, not shelved. Today's word.
Your line: carry three. Pick three sections of the handbook to keep, and carry them with you, on a card, in your phone, or by heart. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Many people who study the Enchiridion keep a few favorite sections written on a card or in a notebook and return to them daily, as Arrian intended the book to be kept at hand.

original.note: Greek: something in the hand, a handbook, or a small dagger kept close.

trapdoor: what you thought: we finished a book.
what it means: the handbook was made to be carried, so the last step is choosing which sections to keep.
what a scholar hears: Arrian's enchiridion, drawn from his teacher's lessons, ends with Cleanthes, Euripides and Socrates; the Discourses come next.
